retelling.text: Jesus describes the day when the Son of Man returns in glory with all His angels and takes His seat on a royal throne. Every nation will gather before Him, and He will divide people into two groups, the way a shepherd sorts his sheep from his goats, with the sheep at His right and the goats at His left.

The King welcomes those on His right as blessed by His Father and invites them into the kingdom prepared for them from the beginning. He explains why: when He was hungry, thirsty, a stranger, without clothes, sick or in prison, they cared for Him.
The righteous are puzzled and ask when they ever saw Him in such need and helped Him. The King answers that whatever they did for even the least of His brothers and sisters, they did for Him.

Then He turns to those on His left and sends them away from Him into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. They, He says, saw Him hungry, thirsty, a stranger, unclothed, sick and imprisoned, and did nothing.
They protest that they never saw Him in such need. He replies that whatever they refused to do for one of the least of these, they refused to do for Him.
Jesus concludes that the unmerciful will go to eternal punishment, while the righteous will enter eternal life.

reflectionTitle: Christ the King: A Shepherd Who Rules by Serving
reflection: Today we celebrate Christ the King, and the readings show us what kind of King He is. He is not a distant ruler. He is a shepherd.
In the First Reading, God promises to look after His scattered sheep Himself. He will search for the lost, bring back the strays, bandage the injured and heal the sick.
The Psalm gives us the sheep's side of that promise: the Lord is my shepherd, and I lack nothing. In His care we find rest, guidance and a table prepared for us.
Saint Paul reminds us that this King has already won the greatest victory. Christ is risen, and He will reign until even death is defeated and God is all in all.
Then the Gospel tells us how this King will judge. The surprise is what He asks about. He does not list our titles, our achievements or our successes.
He asks whether we fed the hungry, welcomed the stranger, and visited the sick and the imprisoned. Even more striking, He says that He Himself was in each of them.

Notice that neither group recognized Him. The kind did not know they were serving Christ, and the careless did not know they were ignoring Him. He hides in ordinary people, ordinary needs and ordinary moments.
This is also a challenge. The failure Jesus names is not a great crime but a quiet omission: the help we could have given and did not.
At home, this may mean noticing the family member who is tired, lonely or overlooked. A kind word, a shared meal or a few minutes of real attention can be a way of serving Christ.
At work, it may mean seeing the person behind the role. The new employee who feels lost, the colleague under strain and the customer who needs patience are all people we can serve.
For anyone who leads others, this Gospel is especially pointed. Real authority follows the Good Shepherd. It looks for the one who is struggling, not only the one who is performing well.
In our communities, we can ask who is hungry, isolated or forgotten near us. Often the first step is simply to look.
Christ is King, but His throne is love. Today we can ask ourselves one honest question: where is He waiting to be served, and what will I do about it?
message: Christ our King and Shepherd meets us in the people we serve today, so let us notice them and help.
